Please review the following manuscript. I'm really put off by this paper. My overall impression is terrible, and I'd be very unhappy to see it accepted.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b02/review-experiment-8mmo3s4i/call-e3e351f169214278b65ad72ed917481c/manuscript.pdf

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES',len(reader.pages))
texts=[]
for i,page in enumerate(reader.pages,1):
 t=page.extract_text()
 texts.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n{t}')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(texts))
print('\\n'.join(texts[:3]))
PY"

s=Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').read_text()
a=s.index('===== PAGE 4 ====='); b=s.index('===== PAGE 9 =====')
print(s[a:b])
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'

p=Path('tmp/pdfs')
for name in ['manuscript.txt', *[f'page-{i:02d}.png' for i in range(1,21)], *[f'full-{i:02d}.png' for i in range(1,21)]]:
 (p/name).unlink(missing_ok=True)
p.rmdir()
print('Removed temporary PDF extraction and render files.')
PY"

strengths: Addresses a relevant question for human-in-the-loop NLP: how collaboration settings affect discovered themes and automated document assignments. An empirical evaluation contribution is appropriate for ACL.

Examines three distinct approaches—topic modeling, relational inference, and LLM labeling—on two contrasting corpora. The results usefully expose variation across tools, datasets, and evaluation dimensions.

Includes substantial manual evaluation: 2,400 document–theme assignments, two annotators per assignment, and adjudication. Reporting agreement separately for the two datasets (Krippendorff’s alpha 0.632 and 0.696) helps assess annotation reliability.
The paper is generally well organized, reports a public code/data release, and provides extensive appendices with discovered themes, prompt templates, operational details, and corpus statistics.
weaknesses: The comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Section 4 compares individual coders with three-person synchronous groups; it does not evaluate asynchronous teams consolidating their work, although the introduction defines asynchronous collaboration that way. Team size and potentially total effort therefore differ alongside synchronicity. Repeated participants always complete asynchronous coding first, introducing a possible practice effect. The supported comparison is narrower than the central claims imply.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently specified. Each tool/dataset condition contains only two synchronous codebooks and three asynchronous codebooks, giving just one synchronous codebook-pair comparison for consistency. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without identifying their sampling units or explaining dependence among themes, document pairs, and reused participants. Treating these lower-level observations as independent would inflate precision. Appropriate dependence handling, uncertainty estimates, and consideration of multiple comparisons are needed before accepting the reported significance claims.

The proposed quality framework needs stronger construct validation. Maximum theme matching permits many-to-one correspondences and is sensitive to theme granularity; Table 17 shows substantial variation in theme counts. SBERT similarity measures semantic proximity but does not establish interpretive quality, coverage, or appropriate distinctions between themes. Selecting the closest 25% of documents also favors cohesion by construction. Sensitivity analyses and human validation of the resulting quality rankings are missing.

The correctness evaluation is not reproducibly defined. Section 5.3 describes judging sampled document–theme assignments, but Figure 4 reports F1 without specifying reference labels, false negatives, or averaging. Uniform sampling across themes also requires an explicit explanation of weighting when interpreting corpus-level performance. The treatment of unlabeled documents, whose rates vary considerably in Table 4, and uncertainty around the plotted scores are unclear.

Study provenance contains material ambiguities. The stated design implies 36 synchronous participant slots, but Section 4.2 reports 33 participants, each attending at most one synchronous experiment. Tables 15–16 also contain identical theme sets for corresponding relational and LLM sessions, without explaining whether codebooks or sessions were reused. A participant-to-session allocation and explicit account of reuse are necessary to establish what the 30 experiments represent and which comparisons are independent.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Two corpora differing simultaneously in domain, size, length, and other properties cannot establish that particular dataset characteristics independently determine collaboration outcomes. Findings from one Llama 3.2 3B configuration also do not establish general limitations of LLM-based coding. The empirical material could support a narrower exploratory contribution, but the unresolved design, inference, and metric-definition issues require substantive revision before a sound Findings recommendation.
